title: Echoes of Eloise: Inside Michigan's most haunted asylum
excerpt: Paranormal group hosts public investigations at former Eloise Asylum
content:
WESTLAND, Mich. (News 10) - What began as the Wayne County Poorhouse became the Eloise Asylum in 1841. At its peak, the complex had nearly 80 buildings, its own farm and a post office. Today, the site is quiet, but some say signs of its past remain.

For nearly a decade, paranormal investigator Megan Buckley has sought out historic and reportedly haunted sites across the country.

“I fell in love with doing it in person. I realized I would run towards it instead of running away, and I realized I wanted to keep doing this long term,” Buckley said.

Earlier this year, Buckley joined MichiGhost, an investigative group formed in October 2024. The team recently partnered with Eloise Asylum to host public, year-round investigations.

“Our stance is not everything is going to be paranormal. There are sometimes where there is a reasonable, more logical explanation for what is happening. One of those is there might just be an EMF that is naturally occurring. So it’s nice we have this equipment so we can go in and actually measure a space first,” Buckley said.

A facility that mirrored the evolution of American medicine

For nearly a century and a half, Eloise evolved into a facility that mirrored the evolution of American medicine. It was home to North America’s first hospital X-ray unit, music therapy, and treatments including electroshock therapy.

“The thing I am so passionate about Eloise is it’s living history. You’ll walk the building, and you’ll see it looks really how it did back in the day. There are recorded lobotomies that happened here as well, too. So it’s got both sides. It’s history, it’s good and bad,” Buckley said.

For MichiGhost, the goal goes beyond goosebumps and jump scares. The group uses sensors and recorders at the site.

“We were coming back to our home base just to kind of get some water and recharge. And we heard a very sharp whistle, like someone whistling at us. So we walkie-talkied the security guard and he said it’s not him but a very common claim here. I have people who are coming back and returning to Eloise and they’ll be saying ‘I had that happen too,’” Buckley said.

Public investigations open to skeptics

Public investigations allow participants to see for themselves. Participants must be above the age of 18. The team says it welcomes doubt as part of uncovering the truth.

“We also have people on our team that don’t believe in ghosts, they keep us grounded and rooted in logic. Because that is the biggest thing. We don’t want to go into a place that is reportedly haunted and just assume everything is a spirit,” Buckley said.
